[NASHR:v2p320/r9] NASHR, d. 833 · ابن ذكوان وحفص والبزي | reports | Ibn Dhakwan raises the fāʾ of تلقف; Hafs has sukūn on lām and a light qāf, while the others use jussive and doubled qāf. Al-Bazzi doubles the tāʾ in connected recitation.
[BIQAI-FULL:v5p29/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The staff in Moses’ right hand recalls the staff first mentioned when God asked what it was during their initial meeting. | mentions 20:17
[BIQAI-FULL:v5p29/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The form suggests forceful, energetic swallowing at a speed scarcely perceived; the omitted tāʾ signals that swiftness.
[BIQAI-FULL:v5p29/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The magicians’ display was the product of extensive training and long practice.
[BIQAI-FULL:v5p29/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The indefinite singular a magician’s trick belittles the whole company and denies its work substance, whether made by one magician or many; a plural would stress their number instead.
[BIQAI-FULL:v5p29/r7] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Magic cannot prevail wherever it goes because it produces only what has no reality.
[BIQAI-FULL:v5p29/r8] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The staff swallowed the display without growing thicker, despite the great quantity of ropes and staffs, so witnesses recognized Moses’ truth and the magicians’ falsehood.
[ITQAN:v4p436/r8] ITQAN, d. 911 · ليث | reports | Layth says he heard that passages from 10:81, 7:117–122, and 20:69 cure sorcery when recited over water in a vessel and poured on the bewitched person's head. | mentions 10:81, 7:117, 7:122
[ITQAN:v4p522/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | Jundab ibn ʿAbd Allah reports the Prophet saying to kill a sorcerer if found; the Prophet recited this verse and explained it as meaning the sorcerer does not succeed wherever found.
[BURSEVI:v5p309#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | What is in your right hand means the staff; the deliberately unspecified wording magnifies it and signals that its extraordinary effects distinguish it from ordinary staffs.
[BURSEVI:v5p309#2/r10] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Magicians as a class never attain their aim wherever they practice magic; this completes the reason the staff defeats their work.
[BURSEVI:v5p309#2/r11] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · التأويلات النجمية | reports | Al-Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya reads the staff as God's own making and scheme, while the magicians' work is theirs; their craft cannot prosper against His firm design.
[BURSEVI:v5p309#2/r12] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Worldly success means survival, wealth, power, and honor; afterlife success means permanence without death, wealth without poverty, honor without humiliation, and knowledge without ignorance. Worldly success alone ends in loss.
[BURSEVI:v5p309#2/r13] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Bursevī illustrates the claim with a student who objects to his teacher and later prospers materially but remains a loser; he applies the lesson to wrongdoers and opponents.
[BURSEVI:v5p309#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Talqaf is jussive as the response to the imperative.
[BURSEVI:v5p309#2/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The verb means to gulp or swallow quickly; al-Mufradāt says it can mean taking something by pulling, whether with the mouth or hand.
[BURSEVI:v5p309#2/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The verb is feminine because mā here stands for the staff.
[BURSEVI:v5p309#2/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Ṣunʿ is doing something skillfully: every craft is an act, but not every act is craft, and craft is not attributed to animals or inanimate things as general action is.
[BURSEVI:v5p309#2/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The staff will swallow ropes and sticks whose apparent motion and lightness frightened Moses; calling them what the magicians made belittles their work as deceit.
[BURSEVI:v5p309#2/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Mā can be a relative pronoun or an indefinite description, yielding either what they made or something they made.
[BURSEVI:v5p309#2/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Kayd sāḥir is nominative as the predicate of inna; its indefinite form in an annexation belittles the sorcerer's kind of scheme.
[BURSEVI:v5p309#2/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | A scheme can be praiseworthy or blameworthy, although the word is more commonly used for blameworthy plotting; the same usage tendency applies to istidrāj and makr.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p228#4/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | What is in Moses’ right hand is his staff; the wording recalls God’s earlier question about what he held. | mentions 7:117, 20:17
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p228#4/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · ابن عامر | reports | Ibn ʿAmir has the same form but raises the verb as a new explanatory clause or a circumstantial clause for the agent or object of ألق.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p228#4/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The command completes the prohibition by explaining how Moses will prevail: the staff consumes the falsehood that triggered his hidden fear.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p228#4/r12] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Some argue this proves Moses did not fear people doubting the staff’s miracle, since the reply would otherwise promise their belief; Alusi says the argument merits consideration.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p228#4/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعض المحققين | reports | Some scholars say ambiguity magnifies the staff as beyond familiar staffs and their ordinary effects, with strange consequences beyond human understanding.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p228#4/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The same effect can be present when another passage narrates the order by meaning; this wording suits removing Moses’ fear and encouraging him. | mentions 7:117
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p228#4/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو حيان | rejects | Abu Hayyan says right hand evokes good fortune and blessing; Alusi objects that the address to Moses was not in Arabic.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p228#4/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Another view takes the ambiguity as belittling the many ropes and staffs: a little stick will consume them; Alusi says this ignores the staff’s earlier extraordinary state.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p228#4/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | ما may be relative or descriptive; one analysis pairs the first possibility with the first construction and the second with the second.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p228#4/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The majority reading is jussive as an answer to the command; from لقف, it means to take deftly by hand or mouth, here by mouth, with feminine agreement because ما refers to the staff.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p228#4/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The staff swallows ropes and staffs whose motion only seemed real; calling them what the magicians made belittles them and signals deception.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p228#4/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Most readers pronounce تلقف with an open lām and doubled qāf, dropping one of the two tāʾs from تتلقف.
[ALUSI-FULL:v16p229/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | This clause explains why the staff swallows their work; ما may mean what they made, a thing they made, or their making.

[ALUSI-FULL:v16p229/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Though الساحر could be definite yet generic, there is no need to identify the magic’s kind: the preceding context does so and the point is its unreality. | mentions 20:66

[TABATABAI:20:49-79#10/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | A sorcerer gains only an illusion for observers, so an unreal undertaking cannot yield genuine success or happiness; this is the major premise behind the claim that sorcerers do not prosper.
[TABATABAI:20:49-79#10/r2] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The claim that sorcerers do not prosper resembles statements that God does not guide wrongdoers and derives from the principle that falsehood vanishes and God effaces it while establishing truth. | mentions 28:50, 61:5, 17:81, 42:24
[TABATABAI:20:49-79#10/r3] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Falsehood keeps embellishing itself as truth, but truth eventually erases it; Moses' staff swallowing the magic illustrates a pattern applying to every falsehood and the truth that destroys it. | mentions 13:17
[TABATABAI:20:49-79#9/r4] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Calling the staff what is in Moses' right hand points to the lack of intrinsic reality in things: by God's will it can be a staff or a living serpent.
[TABATABAI:20:49-79#9/r5] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Calling the magicians' serpents what they made frames the contest as God's unrestricted power against human fabrication, which is false and vanishing before God's word.
[TABATABAI:20:49-79#9/r6] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | The staff's swallowing displays Moses' superiority to the senses, while the verse's conclusion displays his superiority in reality because falsehood has no reality and truth need not fear it.
